title: Best Dog Dental Chews 2026: 5 Brands Tested for Plaque & Safety
description: We tested 5 dog dental chews for plaque reduction, ingredient quality & palatability. Best overall: Greenies. VOHC-accepted, all-natural & enzymatic options compared.
lede: Dental disease affects over 80% of dogs by age three, and most owners don't realize it until bad breath becomes unavoidable or a vet finds significant tartar during a routine checkup. Brushing is the gold standard, but daily brushing compliance is low. Dental chews are the practical middle ground — not as effective as brushing but meaningfully better than nothing when used consistently. These five were evaluated on whether they actually reduce plaque and tartar, not just on whether dogs enjoy eating them.

sections.heading: How to Choose Dog Dental Chews
paragraphs: The Veterinary Oral Health Council (VOHC) is the independent certification body that validates dental claim products. A VOHC seal means the product has been tested in controlled studies and shown to reduce plaque or tartar by at least 10%. That's the baseline to look for — without it, you're relying on marketing claims rather than evidence.

subsections.heading: VOHC Acceptance
paragraphs: The VOHC Accepted seal is the most reliable indicator that a dental chew actually works. Greenies, Virbac CET VeggieDent, and Whimzees all carry VOHC acceptance. Arm & Hammer and Pet MD do not — which doesn't mean they're ineffective, but it means their claims haven't been validated by independent study. For evidence-based purchasing, VOHC acceptance should weigh heavily.

subsections.heading: Ingredient Safety
paragraphs: Rawhide and certain compressed chews carry choking and intestinal blockage risks, particularly for aggressive chewers. Dental chews should be digestible — the VOHC-accepted options here are all formulated to be safely digestible. Check the hardness: chews that don't flex at all when you press them can fracture teeth. The '10-second rule' is a useful guide: if the chew doesn't give within 10 seconds of firm thumb pressure, it's too hard.

subsections.heading: Caloric Content
paragraphs: Dental chews contribute to daily calorie intake. A large Greenie has roughly 90 calories; for a 20lb dog eating 400 calories per day, that's 22% of daily intake from one chew. Count dental chew calories as treats and reduce meal portions accordingly. Virbac VeggieDent and Whimzees have lower caloric density than Greenies.

subsections.heading: Size Matching
paragraphs: Dental chews come in sizes keyed to dog weight. Using a too-small chew on a large dog creates choking risk — the dog may gulp it without chewing. Using a too-large chew isn't a safety risk but reduces the dental benefit (the scraping action happens from chewing, not swallowing). Match the size listed on the package to your dog's weight, and supervise the first few chews with any new product.

sections.heading: Bottom line
paragraphs: Greenies are the evidence-backed default recommendation — VOHC acceptance, wide availability, and strong palatability mean most dogs will actually eat them consistently. Virbac CET VeggieDent is the pick for dogs with food sensitivities or owners who want a grain-free option backed by veterinary branding. Whimzees are the best natural ingredient option with VOHC acceptance. Arm & Hammer is the budget pick for households where cost matters more than certification.

faqs.q: Do dog dental chews actually work?
faqs.a: The VOHC-accepted ones do — with 10–25% reductions in plaque and tartar shown in controlled studies. They work through the mechanical scraping action of chewing combined with any active ingredients (enzymes, antibacterials). They're significantly less effective than daily brushing, but for owners who can't brush daily, a VOHC-accepted chew used consistently makes a measurable difference.

faqs.q: How often should I give my dog dental chews?
faqs.a: Daily use is recommended for maximum benefit — most dental chews are formulated and tested on a daily use basis. Once every few days provides some benefit but less than daily use. Greenies and most VOHC-accepted chews are calorie-counted to be safe for daily use when given in the correct size.

faqs.q: Are dental chews safe to give without supervision?
faqs.a: Supervise the first few times you introduce any new dental chew to understand your dog's chewing style. Dogs who gulp food quickly are at higher choking risk than methodical chewers. Once you've confirmed your dog chews rather than gulps, most dogs can have dental chews without constant supervision. Always remove any pieces smaller than a palm from aggressive chewers.

No. Brushing removes plaque from the full tooth surface including below the gum line; dental chews primarily affect the visible crown. Dental chews are a useful supplement to brushing or a meaningful improvement over no dental care at all — but they don't replicate brushing's effect on gum health and subgingival plaque.

faqs.q: What other options exist for dog dental health?
faqs.a: Water additives (added to the dog's bowl) have some VOHC-accepted options. Dental wipes let you mechanically clean without a full brush. Dental diets (Hill's t/d, Royal Canin Dental) use kibble geometry to scrape teeth. Plaque control sprays work topically. For severe tartar buildup, professional dental cleaning under anesthesia is the only option — chews can't reverse significant existing buildup.

products.review: Greenies are the category benchmark for a reason: VOHC accepted for both plaque and tartar reduction, widely available, and consistently eaten by dogs who refuse other dental products. The texture is designed to flex rather than shatter — safe for regular use. At $24 for 36 regular-size chews, the daily cost is manageable. The ingredient list is relatively clean with wheat as the primary carbohydrate; there's a grain-free version for dogs with wheat sensitivities. Palate acceptance is the highest of any option here — dogs who won't eat other dental chews usually eat Greenies.
pros: VOHC accepted for both plaque AND tartar reduction
Highest palatability — dogs reliably eat them
Flexible texture — appropriate hardness for daily use
cons: Contains wheat — not appropriate for wheat-sensitive dogs
Higher calorie content than some alternatives

products.review: Virbac CET VeggieDent carries VOHC acceptance and is manufactured by a veterinary pharmaceutical company — the brand carries more clinical weight than consumer pet brands. The formula is grain-free (based on rice starch and potato) and uses C.E.T. Dual Enzyme technology to enzymatically target plaque bacteria. At $30 for 30 chews it's mid-range priced. The shape is specifically designed to reach the back teeth where most tartar accumulates. For dogs with grain sensitivities who need a clinically supported option, VeggieDent is the pick.
pros: Veterinary brand with enzymatic antibacterial action
cons: Lower palatability than Greenies for some dogs
Must be given at a specific rate — not as flexible

products.review: Whimzees Brushzees have the cleanest ingredient list of any VOHC-accepted dental chew: potato starch, glycerin, powdered cellulose, and natural colorings — no artificial additives, no meat by-products. VOHC accepted. The toothbrush shape is genuinely functional — the bristle-like projections create multiple cleaning surfaces. At $20 for 24 chews it's the most affordable VOHC-accepted option here. For owners who prioritize natural ingredients without compromising on dental efficacy, Whimzees is the answer.
pros: Cleanest ingredient list of VOHC-accepted options
cons: Vegan formula — no animal protein, lower palatability for some dogs
Softer texture may not satisfy heavy chewers

products.review: Arm & Hammer's dental chews use baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) as the active ingredient — a mild abrasive and odor neutralizer with a track record in human dental products. Not VOHC accepted, but the mechanical abrasive action combined with baking soda provides measurable cleaning versus no dental care at all. At $14 for 28 chews, it's the most affordable option here. The texture is firmer than Greenies, which suits dogs who chew methodically. For budget-conscious owners who want some dental benefit without paying for VOHC-accepted pricing, Arm & Hammer is reasonable.
pros: Baking soda provides additional abrasive cleaning
Widely available at grocery and hardware stores
cons: Not VOHC accepted — no independent efficacy validation
Firmer texture may not suit all dogs

products.review: Pet MD's enzymatic dental chews use glucose oxidase and lactoperoxidase — the same enzymes found in veterinary enzymatic toothpastes — to break down plaque bacteria. Not VOHC accepted, but the enzymatic approach is validated in the broader veterinary dental literature. At $18 for 30 chews it's competitively priced. The chews are softer than most competitors, which makes them appropriate for senior dogs with worn teeth. The chicken flavor has high palatability. For owners who specifically want enzymatic action in a soft chew, Pet MD fills a gap not well covered by the VOHC-accepted options.
pros: Enzymatic action validated in veterinary literature
Softer texture — appropriate for seniors and delicate teeth
cons: Softer texture provides less mechanical scraping than firmer chews

methodology: Dental chews were assessed on VOHC acceptance status, active ingredient mechanism, ingredient quality and safety, caloric content relative to serving, palatability reports, appropriate hardness, size range availability, and value per daily serving.
pinDescription: 80% of dogs have dental disease by age 3. These 5 dental chews are ranked by actual plaque reduction evidence — not just whether dogs like eating them.
